paragraphs: If you are willing to clarify the system's functional and non-functional requirements (performance, security and scalability) before making architectural tradeoffs, this occupation is worth exploring further; choosing a platform immediately or copying a solution can create a large gap between expectations and reality.

If you accept that architectural decisions involve balancing cost, compatibility, maintainability and security, and documenting the reasoning behind tradeoffs, you will use that ability every day in this work; expecting to pursue technical optimization alone without considering constraints will lead to disappointment.

If you are willing to repeatedly confirm component compatibility and interfaces with engineers, developers, operations staff and vendors, and accept that deployment and verification require duty coverage, this work suits you; designing alone without participating in implementation will be difficult to adapt to.

If you are willing to update design documents and installation instructions after changes and retain a rollback plan, this occupation is worth exploring further; undocumented changes can directly become production incidents.

If you are willing to keep tracking platforms, components and security advisories and turn them into architectural and patching decisions, you can sustain this work over time; stopping updates will quickly make solutions and risk controls obsolete.
Before starting, confirm that you can divide system requirements into functional, performance, security and maintainability categories and explain the reasoning behind tradeoffs.

Try it: write a one-page proposal for a fictional scenario (such as converting an internal approval system to a multi-tenant architecture), including the current and target states, components and interfaces, failures and rollback, and three risks and verification methods.

The six judgments are editorial advice; 28 tasks comprise 27 Core/1 Supplemental. The first five scores 81/80/80/79/77 measure importance, not frequency, and include management/budgeting/development; do not exclude overlaps based on the architecture label.
Judgment One: Are System Requirements Clearly Documented?

Record functional and non-functional requirements (performance, availability, security and maintainability) separately and confirm priorities; documenting functions without constraints leaves architectural tradeoffs without a basis.
Judgment Two: Can Component Choices Be Sustained?
Evaluate component licensing, lifecycle, community and vendor support, cost and lock-in risk rather than considering only whether current functionality is sufficient.
Judgment Three: Are Interfaces and Data Flows Clear?
Document interface methods, data flows, failure handling and retry strategies, and confirm both parties' responsibility boundaries and monitoring methods.
Judgment Four: Are Security and Scalability Verifiable?
Turn security requirements and capacity targets into measurable acceptance criteria (such as concurrency, recovery time and log retention) and arrange tests.
Judgment Five: Is Someone Accountable for Deployment and Rollback?
Clarify rollback conditions, data backups and accountable parties before deployment, and prepare switching and verification steps; production changes require approval under organizational processes.
Judgment Six: Are Changes and Documentation Synchronized?
Update design documents, installation instructions and configuration records after architectural changes so colleagues can reproduce the environment from the documentation.

Computer systems engineers and architects design and develop solutions to complex application, systems administration and network problems, perform systems management and integration, and take responsibility for architectural tradeoffs and integration results.

Managers are accountable for departmental resources and delivery; this occupation is accountable for architecture and integration design and does not hold departmental budget or staffing decision authority.
If you prefer coordinating resources and teams and taking responsibility for delivery, explore management; if you prefer going deeper into architecture and integration, explore this occupation.

Project management specialists are accountable for scope, schedule and risk processes; this occupation is accountable for technical architecture and integration solutions, with schedule management one element of collaboration.
If you prefer managing scope and schedule and coordinating resources, explore project management; if you prefer technical solutions and architectural tradeoffs, explore this occupation.

Systems analysts focus on converting requirements into specifications; this occupation focuses on architectural design, component selection and integration verification, taking responsibility for technical solutions.
If you prefer working closely with the business to clarify requirements, explore systems analysis; if you prefer technical architecture and integration, explore this occupation.

Security analysts are accountable for controls and incident response; this occupation must meet security requirements when designing architecture but does not define security policy.
If you prefer studying attack surfaces and establishing security controls, explore security; if you prefer system and architecture solutions, explore this occupation.

Information Security Analysts

Network support specialists focus on operating and maintaining network equipment and links; this occupation focuses on architecture and integration design and usually does not perform routine duty coverage.
If you prefer network operations, maintenance and troubleshooting, explore network support; if you prefer architecture and solution design, explore this occupation.
Maintain networks and equipment, handle connectivity and fault issues, and produce maintenance and handling records.

Administrators are accountable for system availability and routine maintenance; this occupation is accountable for architectural design and integration results and does not perform continuous operational duty coverage.
If you prefer taking responsibility for continuous system operation, explore administration; if you prefer architecture and integration, explore this occupation.
Install, configure and maintain networks, servers and operating systems, producing available systems and operational records.
Network and Computer Systems Administrators

Find a public architecture explanation or system design document, mark requirements, components, interfaces and failure handling, and note three points you want to confirm.
Day 2: Write a Requirements and Constraints Checklist
For the fictional scenario of departmental self-service approval workflow configuration, write functional and non-functional requirements (availability, security and auditing).

Choose three candidate component categories (databases, messaging or configuration centers), compare licensing, support periods and lock-in risks, and write a one-page conclusion.
Day 4: Draw Interfaces and Data Flows
Document one interface's data flow, failure handling and retry strategy, marking responsibility boundaries.
Day 5: Write a Rollback Plan
For a configuration change, document rollback conditions, backup methods and verification steps.

Turn security and capacity targets into 6 measurable acceptance items and corresponding test cases.

Return to this page's judgment checklist and record three reasons to continue and two conditions requiring caution.

entries: Concrete change: can you write an implementable architecture proposal with rollback under constraints rather than merely listing component names?
Facts and choices: do you prefer requirements and solutions, architecture and integration, or platforms and security?
Exercise effort: which step—component comparison, interface design, rollback or acceptance documentation—takes the most out of you, and can you accept repeating it in projects?
Material boundaries: exercises use fictional materials or public information; do not include real company architecture details, accounts or credentials.
Response to feedback: when your design is found to lack failure handling, are you willing to add it consistently to the documentation?
Interest in the process: are you willing to make configuration, verification and documentation reviewable even in projects with no new tools?

Next step: if you are willing to continue after all six previous steps, complete a design-to-deployment cycle with a de-identified real scenario and request peer review. If a step is particularly draining, narrow the direction before further verification.
